summary: Defines an OSPF Router Information TLV that lets routers flood their hostname-to-Router-ID mapping across the network, giving a simple dynamic way to learn names, as IS-IS routers can.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers are known by numbers, which are hard to read. This lets each router announce its human-friendly name.

questions: what is the ospf dynamic hostname tlv
how do ospf routers learn hostnames
subtitle: A new OSPF TLV lets each router announce its own hostname so operators can read names instead of Router IDs.

tldr.problem: OSPF identifies routers by 32-bit Router IDs, which are hard for people to read, and keeping manual name tables on every router does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: Each router puts its hostname in a new Dynamic Hostname TLV (type 7) inside its Router Information Opaque LSA, which is flooded to the other routers.
tldr.outcome: Routers that understand the TLV can build a name-to-Router-ID table automatically, and routers that do not understand it ignore it. The same approach works for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

today: RFC 5642 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the OSPF Dynamic Hostname TLV.

sections.title: Why Router Names Help
sections.content:
OSPF uses a 32-bit Router ID to identify each node. Operators checking adjacencies, routing table entries and the link state database find numerical Router IDs, in dotted-decimal or hexadecimal, less clear than symbolic names.

One fix is a hostname-to-Router-ID table on each router. If built by static definitions, it must list every router on every router, and updating it after additions, deletions or changes is manual, tedious and error prone. This RFC provides a way to fill such tables automatically, and it applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading a list of numbers to find a friend is slow. A list of names is much easier, and this makes the names show up by themselves.

sections.title: Three Ways to Map Names
sections.content:
The RFC compares three approaches.

  • Static tables: the administrator must keep an entry for every router on every router, so it suffers from maintainability and scalability problems.
  • A central service such as DNS: it is a single point of failure, may not resolve names exactly when the network has problems, and can be slow. An operator may also want names different from DNS, or new routers may not yet be in DNS. In native IPv6 OSPFv3 deployments the 32-bit Router ID will not map to an IPv4-addressed entity and will not be DNS resolvable.
  • The protocol itself: carry the mapping in a TLV in the Router Information (RI) LSA from RFC 4970. This is the solution the document defines. Routers that do not understand the TLV ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: You could write names on a paper list by hand, ask one far-away phone book, or have everybody wear a name tag. The RFC picks name tags.

sections.title: The Dynamic Hostname TLV
sections.content:
The Dynamic Hostname TLV is carried in the Router Information Opaque LSA of RFC 4970, for both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. It is OPTIONAL, and a receiving router may ignore it or install the name and Router ID in its hostname table.

The TLV has a 16-bit Type (7), a 16-bit Length and a Hostname value. Length is the length of the hostname in octets, not counting padding. The hostname is 1 to 255 octets, padded with zeroes to 4-octet alignment, in US-ASCII, and is not null-terminated.

The name identifies the router that originated the LSA, and its Router ID comes from the Advertising Router field of the LSA header. The name may be the FQDN for the Router ID, part of it, or any string the operator wants. Using the FQDN or a subset is strongly recommended so the OSPF name and the DNS name can be correlated. If a configuration interface allows Unicode, that interface must apply the ToASCII and ToUnicode algorithms of RFC 3490.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag has a small label saying 'this is a name,' a number saying how long the name is, and then the name itself, padded out so everything lines up neatly.

sections.title: Flooding Scope and Multiple Instances
sections.content:
The TLV MAY go in an area-local or AS-scope RI LSA, but SHOULD NOT be advertised into an area in more than one RI LSA. Area scope uses an OSPFv2 Type 10 RI LSA, or an OSPFv3 RI LSA with S1 set and S2 clear. AS scope uses a Type 11 RI LSA, or an OSPFv3 RI LSA with S1 clear and S2 set.

A router that sends any other AS-scope LSA SHOULD send the hostname in AS scope, and otherwise in area scope. So an ASBR sends an AS-scope TLV, while ABRs and internal routers send an area-scope one. If the TLV does appear in more than one LSA, the hostname SHOULD be the same.

When the RI LSA is advertised in multiple OSPF instances, the hostname SHOULD either be preserved or share a common base, and instances may use consistent prefixes or suffixes for debugging.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can wear its name tag for just its own neighborhood or for the whole town. It should wear one tag per neighborhood, and the name on every tag should match.

sections.title: Security and IPv6 Considerations
sections.content:
Names come from the routers themselves, so a misconfigured or compromised router can inject false mappings, including a duplicate name for different Router IDs. The information should be treated with suspicion during diagnostics of a suspected security incident. The protocol has no generic conflict detection or resolution, although a router that sees its own name from another router can raise a notification or management alert.

Using an FQDN may expose geographic or commercial information when sent in the clear. OSPFv3 supports confidentiality through transport mode IPsec (RFC 4552), and OSPFv2 could run over IPsec tunnels. The RFC encourages authentication for OSPF.

On the IPv6 side, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 both use 32-bit Router IDs. In networks with no native IPv4 interfaces the ID must be set explicitly or derived without collisions, and since it will not map to IPv4 entities or be DNS resolvable, the RFC considers a human-readable mapping extremely desirable.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag is only as honest as the person wearing it. A router could lie about its name, so you should not trust names blindly, especially when hunting for a problem.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the hostname in octets, excluding padding.

fields.name: Hostname ...
fields.desc: 1 to 255 octets of US-ASCII, zero padded to 4-octet alignment.
